ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, there is a uniform electric field in the first quadrant along the positive direction of the $x$-axis, and a uniform electric field in the second quadrant along the negative direction of the $y$-axis. The magnitudes of the electric field strengths in both quadrants are equal. A charged particle with mass $m$ and charge $-q$ is launched from point $P(-L, 0)$ on the $x$-axis with an initial velocity $v_{0}$ into the second quadrant. It is known that the charged particle moves in a straight line in both the first and second quadrants and can pass through the same point $Q$ on the $y$-axis (not shown) twice consecutively. The gravitational acceleration $g$ is a known quantity.

1. The initial velocity $v_{0}$ forms an angle with the positive direction of the $x$-axis.
2. The potential difference $U_{P Q}$ between points $P$ and $Q$
3. The time taken for a charged particle to move in the first quadrant

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the coordinate axes take O as the origin, the x-axis points to the right, and the y-axis points upward. In the second quadrant on the left, vertically downward uniform electric field arrows are drawn; in the first quadrant on the right, horizontally rightward uniform electric field arrows are drawn. Point P is on the negative x-axis, labeled P(-L,0), and the initial velocity v0 emitted from P is obliquely toward the upper right, entering the second quadrant and pointing in the direction of the y-axis. Reasoning: Suppose the magnitudes of the electric field strengths in the two quadrants are both E, and the angle between the initial velocity v0 and the positive direction of the x-axis is θ. The particle charge is -q. In the second quadrant, the electric field direction is downward, so the direction of the electric field force on the negatively charged particle is upward, with magnitude qE; gravity mg is downward. The particle moves in a straight line from P to Q in the second quadrant, and there is no acceleration in the horizontal direction and the horizontal velocity is not zero, so the resultant acceleration in the vertical direction must be zero: qE=mg. Therefore, from P to Q, the magnitude and direction of the particle's velocity remain unchanged. If Q=(0,h), then by the straight-line geometric relation h=L tanθ. After entering the first quadrant, the electric field direction is to the right, and the electric field force on the negatively charged particle is to the left, with magnitude qE=mg; gravity is still downward, so the acceleration is a=(-g,-g). The particle also moves in a straight line in the first quadrant, and when entering from Q, the velocity components are (v0 cosθ, v0 sinθ). To make the trajectory still be a straight line, the acceleration must be collinear with and opposite to the velocity, so v0 sinθ / v0 cosθ = 1, that is, tanθ=1, hence θ=45°. Thus h=L. The potential difference U_PQ=φP-φQ=∫_P^Q E·dl. In the second quadrant, the electric field is vertically downward, and the vertical displacement from P to Q is h, so ∫_P^Q E·dl=-Eh. Also E=mg/q and h=L, so U_PQ=-mgL/q. In the first quadrant, the particle first advances along the 45° direction and then returns to Q. When entering Q, the speed is still v0, and the magnitude of the deceleration along the direction of motion is |a|=√2 g. Therefore, the time from the first passing through Q to passing through Q again is 2v0/(√2 g)=√2 v0/g. Final answer: θ=45°; U_PQ=-mgL/q; motion time in the first quadrant t=√2 v0/g.
